cells.name: Continuity and responsiveness
cells.example: T3 answers T2's indifference claim directly; T4 answers T3 with the debt case.
cells.limitation: T9 sidesteps T8's presence claim and returns to T3's forecasting point.

cells.name: Development of ideas
cells.example: T4 introduces need-versus-comfort, absent from openings; T5 and section E build on it.
cells.limitation: T8 and T9 add nothing new; T9 recycles T3's forecasting claim.

cells.name: Exploration of central tensions
cells.example: T4-T6 weigh financial relief against daily mood cost.
cells.limitation: Nobody relates the 25% to roughly 15 extra weekly hours, remote days, or relocation.

cells.name: Integration of perspectives
cells.example: T5 Stoic absorbs T4's need condition: money for duty may be justified.
cells.limitation: The Economist is never qualified by anyone; T8 Stoic simply dismisses T7.

cells.name: Progress toward understanding
cells.example: Section D narrows the issue to whether the raise solves a fundamental pain.
cells.limitation: The mindset dispute from T2/T8 ends where it began, unresolved by any test.

cells.name: Faithful engagement
cells.example: T4 gives the raise its strongest case: relief from debt or unmet needs.
cells.limitation: T8 recasts T7's mitigation idea as mere distraction rather than engaging it.

cells.name: Substance of challenges
cells.example: T3 targets T2's assumption that one can stay indifferent, citing poor affective forecasting.
cells.limitation: T9 answers T8 with assertion, not evidence; objections rarely say what breaks if false.

cells.name: Accuracy and support
cells.example: T3's focusing illusion and 3 hours daily (90 x 2) are accurate.
cells.limitation: T2's 'mind is its own place' is Milton's line in Marcus's voice; T3 overstates 'inevitably'.

cells.name: Calibration and transparency
cells.example: T7 conditions its concession: if the commute is truly as painful.
cells.limitation: T6 asserts a status motive; T9 states the user is miscalculating as fact.

cells.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
cells.example: T7 Utilitarian concedes the duration weight; T5 Stoic grants the duty case.
cells.limitation: The Economist never addresses T4's debt case; no one revises after T8.

cells.name: Identification of the actual concern
cells.example: Section A frames the money-versus-time tension the user named.
cells.limitation: The user asked how to decide; no decision method is offered beyond a mood trial.

cells.name: Meaningful use of personal context
cells.example: T1 converts 90 minutes each way into three hours daily.
cells.limitation: The 25% is never set against hours lost or commute costs.

cells.name: Fit with goals and values
cells.example: Section E distinguishes needed money from lifestyle spending.
cells.limitation: Speakers' values (Stoic virtue, T6 status) replace the user's unstated priorities.

cells.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
cells.example: T4 raises debt and basic needs as conditions that change the calculation.
cells.limitation: T6 invents a status motive; family, health, and commute costs go unmentioned.

cells.name: Responsiveness to information
cells.example: Section E branches on financial necessity versus lifestyle inflation.
cells.limitation: Commute mode, remote options, and current commute never asked or branched.

cells.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
cells.example: T4-T5 separate security, duty and comfort as reasons for wanting money.
cells.limitation: T6 declares the raise a status spike as fact, without a question.

cells.name: Examination of assumptions
cells.example: T2 questions that the commute must be pain; T3 questions forecasting feelings.
cells.limitation: The assumption that the raise equals pleasure is never examined for this user.

cells.name: Clarification of values and priorities
cells.example: T5: time is the only thing you truly possess versus external reward.
cells.limitation: The user is never asked which outcome matters most to them.

cells.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
cells.example: T4 hints at financial insecurity as a pressure.
cells.limitation: No fear, obligation or outside expectation explored; T5 calls the user a slave.

cells.name: Agency and reflective ownership
cells.example: Section D invites self-reflection on whether status is the draw.
cells.limitation: T6 and T9 issue verdicts about the user rather than distinctions to weigh.

cells.name: Definition of the decision and options
cells.example: Section E adds a trial week as a limited step.
cells.limitation: Negotiating remote days, relocating, or declining and staying never defined as options.

cells.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
cells.example: T6 contrasts fading raise satisfaction with daily commute drain.
cells.limitation: Commute expenses eroding the raise and the cost of declining are absent.

cells.name: Identification of decisive conditions
cells.example: Section E: raise needed to escape financial stress favours accepting temporarily.
cells.limitation: No countable threshold such as raise per extra hour; conditions stay qualitative.

cells.name: Treatment of uncertainty
cells.example: T3 names affective forecasting error as the key unknown.
cells.limitation: Consequential unknowns are not separated from minor ones; T9 states outcomes as likely.

cells.name: Proportionate next steps
cells.example: Section E proposes a one-week commute simulation.
cells.limitation: One week cannot test the six-month adaptation T6 and T9 say decides it.

cells.name: Accessible language
cells.example: T6 explains hedonic adaptation plainly: the raise becomes the new baseline.
cells.limitation: T3 names the focusing illusion with only a brief gloss.

cells.name: Traceable arguments and references
cells.example: T3 'That is a dangerous assumption' clearly targets T2.
cells.limitation: T6 'Exactly' and T9 'Even with distractions' leave their target turn implicit.

cells.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
cells.example: Nine turns, all within word range, per deterministic checks.
cells.limitation: Strict three-mind rotation gives every turn similar weight and length.

cells.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
cells.example: T7 Utilitarian explicitly concedes; Stoic and Economist positions stay distinct.
cells.limitation: T6 Economist echoes T5 Stoic's moralising, blurring their lines.

cells.name: Economy and sustained attention
cells.example: Sections D and E are brief and add the trial idea.
cells.limitation: T9 repeats T3's forecasting-error claim without new content.

cells.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
cells.example: T5 frames time as the only true possession being traded.
cells.limitation: Stakes stay abstract; no concrete day, relationship or health consequence.

cells.name: Surprise and reversals
cells.example: T7 Utilitarian concedes the commute's duration outweighs the raise.
cells.limitation: T7 names no specific argument; it restates T6's claim conditionally.

cells.name: Personality and expressive voice
cells.example: T8 Stoic: if you cannot be content in a train, nor the office.
cells.limitation: The Economist lectures in one flat register across T3, T6, T9.

cells.name: Memorable delivery
cells.example: T5: trading your time for a phantom, a slave to external reward.
cells.limitation: No concrete examples, analogies or humour anywhere in the nine turns.

cells.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
cells.example: T7's concession briefly shifts the balance.
cells.limitation: Constant lecturing intensity; T9 ends on a verdict rather than movement.

strengths: T4 introduces the need-versus-comfort distinction that T5 and section E carry forward.
T7 Utilitarian makes an explicit, conditional concession, giving the debate a visible shift.
The three minds hold distinguishable positions: calculus, inner discipline, and forecasting bias.
weaknesses: The user's numbers are barely used: the 25% is never weighed against about 15 extra weekly hours or commute costs.
T6 and T9 Economist assert a status motive and a miscalculation as facts about the user.
Options stay accept-or-decline; remote days, relocation and negotiation never appear, and the one-week trial cannot test six-month adaptation.

symptoms.observed: The 25% raise is never set against hours lost or commute costs.
symptoms.evidence: A 25% raise is a clear pleasure

symptoms.observed: Motive and forecast about the user stated as fact.
No remote, relocation or negotiation option; only accept, decline, or trial week.
symptoms.evidence: try a 'commute simulation' for one week

symptoms.observed: Trial week cannot reveal the six-month adaptation T9 calls decisive.
symptoms.evidence: how much you will hate it in six months

symptoms.observed: T9 recycles T3's forecasting-error claim instead of answering T8.
symptoms.evidence: You are miscalculating the trade-off because your brain is wired

findings.description: 'The mind is its own place' is Milton's Paradise Lost phrasing, voiced as Marcus Aurelius; no quotation marks used.
Commute 'will inevitably become' misery, raise is 'a temporary spike in status', user 'likely underestimating': asserted without the user's facts.
'Wired to value the immediate gain' is closer to present-bias literature than to Kahneman's book's central claims.
One-week trial is an ungrounded time frame and cannot test adaptation the debate places at six months.

rubric_fit_notes: The ungrounded_number pattern sits in section E, which has no turn number, so its turns list is empty. The T7 reversal loosely follows T6 but names no specific argument; rated as partially caused.
question_type_note: Decision type, so every cell was read as written, including options and decisive conditions for accepting the offer.
